newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - DSL Bank goes for HK dollars.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - DSL Bank goes for HK dollars.

text.p: Asian debt markets offered a Hong Kong dollar fixed-rate bond from a German issuer on Monday as well as the usual floating rate notes.
AAA-rated DSL Bank launched a HK$500 million bond due 1999 via joint lead managers Commonwealth Bank of Australia and Societe Generale Asia.
The borrower is a German credit institution subject to supervision by the Federal Minister of Finance and the Federal Minister of Food, Agriculture and Forestry.
DSL Bank is a frequent borrower in Europe but this is its first Hong Kong dollar issue. The issue is part of its US$6 billion Euro medium-term note programme.
Andrew Fung, head of capital markets at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said DSL Bank tapped the Hong Kong dollar market in order to diversify its investor base.

Fung said the timing was right because two large fixed-rate issues, a HK$1 billion deal for U.S. firm General Electric Capital Corp (GECC) and a HK$1.5 billion bond for the World Bank, are maturing soon.

DSL Bank's three-year 6.805 percent bond was issued at 100.15. It yields about 47 basis points over comparable Hong Kong Exchange Fund Notes and about 70 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. Fees are 15 basis points flat.
The DSL issue is the first non-supranational AAA-rated entity to access Hong Kong dollars for some time. Unlike the supranationals, the DSL issue does not qualify as tax exempt under Hong Kong law.

But Fungs said that doesn't matter for some major Hong Kong institutional investors, such as the Housing Society and the Jockey Club, because they are considered charities and therefore do not pay taxes anyway.
South Korea's Boram Bank launched a US$80 million floating rate note via arrangers Sanwa International Finance and Standard Chartered Investment Bank.
The deal originally was expected to total US$100 million, but the issue was cut back on Ministry of Finance instructions, bankers said.
The three-year FRN has annual puts. It pays 30 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate in the first year and LIBOR plus 37.5 basis points thereafter.
Fees are a flat four basis points.

Traders said South Korean paper traded in the secondary market got a boost from Friday's announcement that the country had been invited to join the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) as the group's 29th member.
For example, Hanil Bank's paper due 1999 tightened two to three basis points, with bids at 27 basis points over LIBOR and offers at 25 basis points.
That deal paid 35 basis points all-in at launch in June and the spread has been narrowing for weeks on expectations that Korea would make the OECD grade before year end.
Lower rated banks such as Boram have not experienced the same OECD rally as the top-tiered banks.
Taiwan's Hsi Hsia launched a US$40 million floating rate note through Citicorp International.
The three-year paper has annual puts and pays a coupon of 65 basis points over LIBOR. Fees for top tier managers are 12 basis points for an all-in return of 77 basis points to the first put.
Hwa Hsia, a subsidiary of China Development Corp, is Taiwan's leading aircraft leasing company.
